children: Stocks are refusing to buckle under the bond selloff — for now.
The bond market sets the price

S&P 500 futures were little changed near 7,705 Friday after the cash index finished Thursday almost perfectly flat. No big news on deck for today, allowing traders to pause and regroup after some wild gyrations over the past few days.
Stocks recovered from sharper intraday losses on reports that the US and Iran were exploring a path toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz (stop us if you’ve heard that, right?).

The bigger move is in bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to roughly 5.19% after touching 5.225%, its highest in 19 years. The 30-year reached 5.50%, a level last seen in 2004, while US mortgage rates have returned to 7%.

Markets now assign a 71% probability to another Fed hike next month, up from 53% earlier this week. More than 90 basis points of additional tightening — almost four standard quarter-point increases — is priced across the cycle. The “one and done” interpretation of September’s hike has aged rather quickly.
Asia holds up, but the pressure is global

Asia produced a mixed session. Japan’s Nikkei gained about 1%, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1% and Australia lost 0.6%. Mainland China, South Korea and Taiwan were closed, leaving the region’s broader index roughly unchanged.

Trump and Xi’s Washington meetings have so far delivered little visible progress on trade, AI, Taiwan or Iran. That absence of a breakthrough weighed on Hong Kong, although markets also avoided the sort of negative surprise that could have created a more aggressive risk-off move.

The bond pressure is no longer exclusively American. Japan’s 10-year yield rose above 3.1%, its highest since 1996, while Australia’s reached 5.4%. Higher global yields raise financing costs and reduce the relative appeal of expensive equities, particularly technology stocks whose expected profits sit further in the future.
Dollar firms as oil keeps inflation alive

The dollar index is heading for a weekly gain of roughly 1% near 101.25, its strongest level since late July. Higher US yields support the dollar but create another headwind for American multinationals by reducing the translated value of revenue earned overseas.

Brent crude eased around 0.8% to $105.75 after surging 3% Thursday following a Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia. Oil is now a crucial S&P 500 input: energy producers benefit from higher prices, but the wider index faces stronger inflation and potentially tighter Fed policy.
Bitcoin held around $84,000 while gold remained weak near $4,270 early Friday morning. Another jump in Treasury yields would make non-yielding gold and speculative crypto assets harder to defend.
AI deals and earnings create stock-level action

Akamai surged in extended trading after signing a seven-year, $11.6 billion cloud-infrastructure agreement with Anthropic. The commitment could expand by another $9 billion, although Akamai expects $5.5 billion of associated capital expenditure.

Costco reported earnings of $6.75 a share on revenue of $95.7 billion, beating forecasts of $6.55 and $94.85 billion. A subdued after-hours reaction suggested investors wanted more than another respectable quarter from a company already carrying a premium valuation.

, while Oracle lost nearly 5% and several semiconductor names weakened under the weight of higher yields.

title: SPX: S&P 500 Futures Hold Flat as Treasury Yields Rise Even More
